'''''Crataegus crus-galli''''' is a species of [[Crataegus|hawthorn]] known by the common names '''cockspur hawthorn''', '''cockspur thorn''', '''Newcastle hawthorne''', '''Newcastle thorn''', '''hog apple'''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Crataegus crus-galli (Cockspur Hawthorn) |url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/crataegus-crus-galli |access-date=2026-02-08 |website=Gardenia |language=en-US}}</ref> It is native to North America and is widely used in [[horticulture]]. It produces edible fruit.

==Description==
This is a small tree growing up to about 10 meters tall and 8 meters wide, rounded in form when young and spreading and flattening as it matures. The leaves are 5 to 6 centimeters long, glossy dark green in color and turning gold to red in the fall. The flowers are white and have a scent generally considered unpleasant. The fruits are small [[pome]]s that vary in colour, usually a shade of red.<ref name="Phippsetal">{{cite book |last1=Phipps |first1=J.B. |url=https://archive.org/details/hawthornsmedlars00jame |title=Hawthorns and medlars |last2=O'Kennon |first2=R.J. |last3=Lance |first3=R.W. |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |year=2003 |isbn=0-88192-591-8 |location=Cambridge, U.K. |url-access=registration}}</ref> Most wild varieties{{specify|date=November 2023}} of the tree are heavily armed in sharp thorns several centimeters long.{{fact|date=November 2023}}

[[File:Cockspur Thorn3.jpg|thumb|A Cockspur Thorn tree in flower, Oxfordshire UK, 5th May 2022.]]

==Taxonomy==
It is thought to be the parent, along with ''[[Crataegus succulenta]]'', of the [[tetraploid]] species ''[[Crataegus persimilis]]''.

==Distribution and habitat==
It is native to eastern North America from [[Ontario]] to [[Texas]] to [[Florida]].<ref name="USDA">{{PLANTS|symbol=CRCR2|taxon=Crataegus crus-galli L.|access-date=7 June 2022}}</ref><ref name="Phippsetal" />

==Cultivation==
This species is a popular [[ornamental plant|ornamental tree]], especially var. ''inermis'', which lacks thorns. Many other wild forms would be very suitable for [[landscaping]] if better known, and [[List of hawthorn species with yellow fruit|yellow-fruited forms]] exist.<ref name=Phippsetal/>

==Uses==
The fruit is edible and can be made into jelly or crushed to make tea.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|pages=237–38|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref>
